query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Eutectic high entropy alloys (EHEAs) can be engineered to exhibit a ductile–brittle–ductile transition by exploiting their unique, hierarchically patterned microstructures and coherent phase interfaces, which avoid conventional temper embrittlement mechanisms seen in traditional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy with a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
generation.intervention: Application of high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment to modify the microstructure.
generation.conditions: Thermal cycling and controlled HPHT processing to induce changes in deformation mechanisms across a specific temperature window.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces that favor multiple deformation mechanisms (dislocations, twins, stacking faults).
generation.mechanism: The HPHT treatment alters the interfacial characteristics and the activation of multiple deformation mechanisms, effectively mitigating stress concentrations that would normally trigger brittle fracture (temper embrittlement). This results in a temperature-dependent transition from ductile to brittle behavior and back to ductile as the dominant deformation mechanisms adjust.
generation.predicted_outcome: An observable ductile–brittle–ductile transition, where the alloy exhibits high ductility at low and high temperatures, with a temporary loss of ductility in an intermediate temperature range; the transition width and magnitude are expected to be tunable via processing parameters.
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys such as tungsten-based heavy alloys typically suffer from temper embrittlement within a narrow temperature window, while similar embrittlement has not been reported in compositionally complex HEA systems.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected to hold for eutectic high entropy alloys with similar dual-phase lamellar microstructures and may be sensitive to variations in alloy composition and specific HPHT processing parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature range for the transition and the quantitative change in ductility are uncertain and may vary with the exact composition and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of samples of a eutectic high entropy alloy with a known dual-phase lamellar microstructure. Subject these samples to a range of controlled HPHT treatments followed by systematic thermal cycling across the suspected ductile–brittle transition temperature range.
measurements: Tensile ductility and yield strength at various temperatures
Microstructural characterization (e.g., using TEM/SEM) to identify interface coherence and phase distributions
Fractography to assess the mode of failure (ductile vs brittle)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated EHEA does not exhibit a reproducible region of reduced ductility at an intermediate temperature (or if the transition can be entirely suppressed by minor processing variations), then the hypothesis that the HPHT-induced microstructure mediates a ductile–brittle–ductile transition in these alloys is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are defined as equimolar or nonequimolar single- and multiphase solid solutions, depending on the number and type of principal/secondary metallic elements with the configurational entropy greater than 1.61 R , (where R is the gas constant) ( [1] , [2] ). The minimization of the Gibbs free energy by increasing the configurational entropy results in the formation of a single- or multiphase solid solution, such as body-centered cubic (BCC) ( [3] ), face-centered cubic (FCC) ( [4] ), and/or hexagonal close-packed solid-solution phases ( [5] ) instead of intermetallic compounds ( [6] ). Moreover, the random distribution of multiple elements with different atomic radii leads to a severely distorted lattice with variations in the interatomic distances along the crystallographic direction of the unit cells ( [3] ). These features, in turn, contribute to desirable mechanical properties, such as high hardness, strength, ductility, and softening resistance at room temperature (RT) and elevated temperatures ( [3] ).
